title: Parkinson admitted upfront that story was made up.
description:
Parkinson admitted upfront that story was made up. The real piece was a satirical nine-page article for The Economist in November 1955, and it's still quoted today as if it were a study.

Officials up 78 percent, while the fleet shrank by two-thirds. It reads like scientific proof. Parkinson never disclosed where the numbers came from.

The true growth was even bigger than Parkinson said, and so was the reason he left out. The honest 1914 baseline was lower, pushing the real increase closer to 120 percent. That surge tracks almost exactly with the paperwork of the First World War, which Parkinson's essay never mentions once.

A serious naval historian, Raffles Professor of History at the University of Malaya, in Singapore, whose nine-page joke in The Economist was collected into a book that sold nearly a quarter of a million copies in two years.

Historian Jon Sumida's corrected 1914-to-1928 growth rate, using the actual Navy Lists rather than Parkinson's undisclosed source.

Sources:
- http://doc.cat-v.org/economics/parkinsons-law/: the original essay text, read in full. Establishes: byline credits "Northcote Parkinson, Raffles Professor of History at the University of Singapore"; first appeared in The Economist in November 1955; opens with the (explicitly illustrative) story of an elderly lady spending a whole day mailing a postcard, an hour finding it, another finding her spectacles, half an hour finding the address, an hour and a quarter composing it, twenty minutes deciding about an umbrella, against a busy person's three minutes; states "Factor I: An official wants to multiply subordinates, not rivals" and "Factor II: Officials make work for each other."
- https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/1994/december-1/challenging-parkinsons-law: Jon Sumida (associate professor of history, University of Maryland), "Challenging Parkinson's Law," Naval History Magazine, December 1994, read in full. Establishes Parkinson's actual career (PhD in history, King's College London; Master of the Royal Naval College Dartmouth; Lecturer in History, Liverpool; Raffles Professor of History at the University of Malaya; died 9 March 1993 aged 83; wrote over 60 books, mostly serious naval history); that the postcard story was "obviously fictitious" by Parkinson's own framing; that the collected book sold nearly a quarter of a million copies in two years; Parkinson's published Admiralty table (1914: 2,000 officials to 1928: 3,569, a 78.45% rise, against a 67.74% fall in capital ships and a 31.5% fall in personnel); that Parkinson never disclosed the source of these statistics; that an independent check against the actual Navy Lists found the true 1914 figure was about a quarter lower than Parkinson's, which raises the honest percentage increase to roughly 120%; and that this growth tracks almost exactly with World War One's demands, wartime equipment failures, a hiring surge to match the Ministry of Munitions' paperwork, and the mass hiring of lower-paid women clerical staff, none of which Parkinson's essay mentions.
